On Sunday, at 3am (2am GMT), Martin Schaefer, the German consul general to Turkey, tweeted to request permission from Turkish authorities to fly a helicopter loaded with more than a dozen German medical professionals—doctors, nurses, and paramedics—to the town of Kobane in northern Syria.
German interior minister Thomas de Maizière stated over the weekend that Ayn al-Arab, locally known as Kobane, urgently required medical supplies and healthcare workers to address the latest conflict between Isis militants and Kurdish military groups.
Turkey has barred all humanitarian relief from entering Syria. The town is besieged by Isis, which have forced tens of thousands of civilians to flee their homes and are preventing any relief from entering the town by mercenaries and fighters under their control.
Speaking on Monday, a foreign affairs spokesman for Merkel’s Christian Democrats said the German interior minister would again ask the Turkish government to authorise the helicopter’s flight to Ayn al-Arab.
At the same time, a coalition commander’s effort to outline a plan for invading ISIS’s self-proclaimed capital of Raqqa has drawn the coalition nearer to finalizing a military strategy for the next stage of the campaign against ISIS.
Up to 50 countries were said to be poised to support the planned operation to regain the ISIS-held city of Raqqa, General Martin E Dempsey, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, disclosed to Congress on Monday. Dempsey said the idea has come from the Pentagon. Speaking before the Senate armed services committee he told senators that:
“We’re about to have the opportunity to get the next phase of our campaign plan into the, what I would call, warrior’s hands - coalition partners who are fully ready to undertake that mission, and they will assault Raqqa.”
